steps: Schematic of the classic five-engine Gravity suit (as described 2020–2022): two micro gas turbines on each forearm, one on the back. The Mk4 (not shown) has three back turbines; its total engine count is not published.

Each engine pushes along its own axis: one arrow per engine. To hover, the upward parts of these thrusts balance the weight of pilot, suit and fuel. The sideways forces and turning moments balance too.

Browning's analogy: the grouped pushes are a teepee of thrust, like the poles of a tent. In his 2021 description of the classic suit, the back engine carries the equipment plus about one third of his body weight; the arms about two thirds.

Reported figures, not computed here: about 144 kgf (317 lbf), AOPA 2020; about 155 kgf for an earlier rig, Browning 2017. These are separate total-thrust reports. Record: 136.891 km/h (85.06 mph), Guinness, 2019-11-14.

The pilot steers by moving the arms to aim the thrust. Here both arms swing back, so the exhaust is aimed back and a forward component of thrust results. The pose is schematic, not a worked manoeuvre.

Inside one engine, cut open: a JetCat-style micro turbojet (schematic example, not confirmed Gravity hardware). The compressor squeezes the air. Fuel burns with oxygen in the compressed air in the combustion chamber.

JetCat-style example, not confirmed Gravity hardware. Hot gas drives the turbine, which turns the compressor on the same shaft. Gas speeds up out of the nozzle; the reaction is thrust. Shaft: about 120,000 rpm (reported).
